objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain and demonstrate a complete preflight assessment of pilot, airplane and environment, and teach a learner to run it with the checklist, find defects, apply the regulations and manage the risks on their own.
why: Hasty ground operations shrink the margin of safety, and safe flight begins and ends on the ground [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Learners copy their instructor's habits whether they mean to or not [[25:164|AIH 8-6]], so the walkaround you teach on lesson one is the one they will still do years later. On the checkride you must do the preflight assessment and explain it at the same time, the way you would to a learner.

warmup: Think first: your new learner walks around the airplane in four minutes, checklist in hand, and says "all good." How would you find out, without doing the walkaround again yourself, whether they actually looked at anything? And what would you check about the learner before you check the airplane?

chunks.title: What a preflight assessment is, and why you teach it from lesson one

body.p: Ground operations are where a pilot sizes up four things before committing: the rules, their own readiness to be pilot in command, the airplane's condition, and the flight environment, plus any outside pressure that could weaken the decision [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Situational awareness starts during preparation and ends only when the airplane is tied down or hangared, or the pilot decides not to go [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

The word to teach first is airworthy. Under 14 CFR 3.5(a), as the AFH quotes it, an airworthy aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Two parts, and a learner needs both:

bullets: Conforms to its type design. The type design is the set of drawings, specifications, materials and airworthiness limitations that define the certificated airplane [[60:44|14 CFR 21.31]]. The airplane and its installed parts must match the original type certificate or an approved altered condition [[24:25|AFH 1-4]].

In condition for safe operation. This is what the walkaround checks today. A standard airworthiness certificate stays valid only while the airplane meets its type design, is in condition for safe operation, and is maintained under Parts 21, 43 and 91 [[24:24|AFH 1-3]].

callout.text: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping the airplane airworthy [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. But no one may operate a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy, and the pilot in command decides whether it is in condition for safe flight and must discontinue the flight if unairworthy conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

body.p: That split is the heart of K2 and S2: the maintenance records tell you what was done, and your eyes tell you what the airplane looks like now. The PHAK calls the preflight inspection a thorough and systematic way to decide whether the airplane is airworthy and in condition for safe operation, and says the POH has a section for it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

callout.text: How to teach it: on the first lesson, present the preflight to make the learner familiar with the airplane and its parts, not as a list of ways to die. A first lesson built on emergencies and dire warnings can make a new learner wonder whether learning to fly is a good idea [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]. But insist on the correct procedure from the very first walkaround: habits are much easier to build right than to fix later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

check.q: Your learner asks: "The annual was signed off last week by a mechanic. Why do I have to check anything?"
check.a: The owner or operator keeps the airplane maintained [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]], but the pilot in command decides whether it is in condition for safe flight today [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. Airworthy means both conforming to type design and being in safe condition [[24:38|AFH 2-1]], and condition can change after any inspection.

chunks.title: Pilot self-assessment: two pilots, two checklists

body.p: Pilots often check the airplane thoroughly and never check themselves. A personal checklist, based on experience, currency and comfort level, does for the pilot what the airplane checklist does for the airplane, and the instructor should teach it that way [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].
Start with capability. The RMH asks three questions [[30:22|RMH 3-4]] [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]:

bullets: Qualification: does the pilot hold the certificate, category, class and ratings needed for this airplane under these conditions [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]?
Currency: are the required takeoffs, landings, approaches and flight review logged, and is that enough for this flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]?
Proficiency: can the pilot really manage the expected conditions? In an unfamiliar airplane, can they run its avionics and systems [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]?

body.p: Then the body and mind, with IMSAFE:

head: IMSAFE item
What the AIH adds
What you watch for in your learner
rows: Illness
An obvious pilot risk [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]
A sick learner is preoccupied and may not have the capacity to learn [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]
Medication
Any medicine that might affect judgment or cause drowsiness [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]
Ask about over-the-counter drugs too; both kinds have side effects [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Stress
Not on the list of grounding conditions in the rules, but it hurts concentration and performance [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]
Work, family and money pressures show up as distraction and anxiety [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Alcohol
Drinking within 8 hours? Within 24? A small amount can impair skills and raise susceptibility to disorientation and hypoxia [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]
Hangover and dehydration can last longer than 8 hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Fatigue
One of the most insidious hazards; it may not show until serious errors are made [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]
Acute fatigue looks like inattention, distractibility, timing errors, neglect of secondary tasks and irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Emotion
Anger, depression and anxiety lower alertness and can lead to risk taking [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]
The pilot may choose not to fly until recovered [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]

callout.text: No one may act as a crewmember within 8 hours after drinking alcohol, while under the influence, while using a drug that affects their faculties contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. A medical certificate holder may not act as PIC while they know or have reason to know of a condition that would make them unable to meet the medical certificate needed [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]].

body.p: Two more ideas to teach. First, legal and safe are different: the regulations set the floor, and safe pilots know the difference [[25:9|AIH 1-5]]. Second, personal minimums come from honest self-assessment. If the AFM shows a 15 knot crosswind component but the pilot has flown only 10 knots, 10 knots is the personal limit until more training [[25:16|AIH 1-12]]. The AIH Personal Minimums Checklist says never to loosen a minimum while planning a specific flight, and not to go with marginal items in two or more risk categories [[25:206|AIH D-1]].

callout.text: During instruction, the P in PAVE applies to both the learner and the instructor [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Run IMSAFE on yourself, and build enough trust that learners tell you about their own aeromedical issues well before the flight, so you can reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: Your learner says, "Rough week at work and not much sleep, but I'm fine." Which two IMSAFE items are in play, and why is "I'm fine" not good enough?
check.a: Stress and fatigue. Stress is not a grounding condition in the rules but it degrades performance [[25:12|AIH 1-8]], and fatigue may not be apparent until serious errors are made [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. Ask questions, watch for acute fatigue signs [[25:47|AIH 2-14]], and be ready to change the lesson.

chunks.title: Is this the right airplane, and is it airworthy?

body.p: "Appropriate" comes before "airworthy." The AIH's aircraft questions: is this the right aircraft for the flight, is the pilot familiar and current in it, is it equipped for the flight, can it use the runways with a margin, carry the load, reach the altitudes, and carry enough fuel with reserves? And does the fuel delivered match the fuel ordered [[25:9|AIH 1-5]]? Remind learners that book performance comes from a new airplane flown by a professional test pilot [[25:9|AIH 1-5]].

Instruction adds its own aircraft hazards. The airplane may not be under your control or maintenance supervision, so you may not know about inoperative equipment or overdue inspections. Two-place trainers often cannot carry full fuel with two people aboard, and performance may be marginal at high density altitude [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

callout.text: The AIH fix: find the airplane's official airworthiness status before the scheduled flight and before the preflight, know the operator's procedure for reporting and fixing discrepancies, read the current discrepancy list, and settle any airworthiness question with maintenance before you start the walkaround. Involve the learner in this [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

body.p: Logbooks are not normally kept in the airplane, so the pilot should review them, or a summary of the airworthy status, before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. A summary sheet like the one below is a good teaching aid:

head: Record item
Requirement
rows: Annual inspection
Within the preceding 12 calendar months [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]
100-hour inspection

For carrying any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft that the instructor provides; up to 10 hours over is allowed only to reach a place to do the inspection, and it counts toward the next 100 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]] [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]
Transponder
Tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months before use [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413]]
ELT

Inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]; battery replaced (or recharged) once the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of its useful life has expired [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]
ADs, life-limited parts, Form 337s
Status and entries checked in the records [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]

body.p: Then the documents in the airplane: an airworthiness certificate and registration [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]], with the airworthiness certificate displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so passengers or crew can read it [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]]; the operating limitations as an AFM/POH, placards and markings [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]; current weight and balance data, a compass correction card if required, and the external data plate [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

Conformity to type design is what S2 asks you to verify. The AFM/POH equipment list, kept current through the Type Certificate Data Sheet, shows the equipment required for airworthiness [[24:25|AFH 1-4]]. After maintenance or alteration, the airplane needs an approval for return to service and the record entry [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. If the work may have appreciably changed how it flies, no one other than crewmembers may be carried until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate flies an operational check and logs it [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]].

callout.text: Two rules that change with the kind of flying you do: the 100-hour applies to carrying people (other than crewmembers) for hire and to instruction for hire in an airplane the instructor provides [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], and the ELT rule does not apply to training operations conducted entirely within 50 NM of the airport where the local flights began [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]].

check.q: The logbook shows an STC for a larger engine than the one listed on the original type certificate. Your learner asks whether the airplane still "conforms to its type design." What do you answer?
check.a: Yes, if the change is an approved alteration. The airplane must conform to the original type certificate or an approved altered condition [[24:25|AFH 1-4]], so check that the alteration and its paperwork are in the records.

chunks.title: Something is inoperative: let the learner decide first

body.p: Under 14 CFR, all installed instruments and equipment are required to work before each departure, unless a legal exception applies. When the walkaround finds something broken, there are three choices: cancel, get maintenance before flight, or defer the item [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. With an approved MEL, the airplane is flown under that MEL and its letter of authorization [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]. Most trainers use the 91.213(d) deferral instead:

head: 91.213(d) step
What it means
rows: The item is not required

Not part of the VFR-day type certification equipment, not required on the equipment list or the kinds of operations equipment list, not required by 91.205 or another rule for this flight, and not required by an AD [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]
Remove or deactivate it

Removed with the cockpit control placarded and the maintenance recorded, or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative"; deactivation that involves maintenance follows Part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]]
Decide it is not a hazard
An appropriately rated pilot, or a person rated to maintain the airplane, determines the item is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]]
Fix it later
The owner has it repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]
Cannot defer?
A special flight permit may still allow a flight to a repair shop [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]]

body.p: So the learner needs to know 91.205. Day VFR needs, among others, an airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator, tachometer, oil pressure and oil temperature gauges, a fuel gauge for each tank [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]], and on small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, an anticollision light system [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)]]. Night VFR adds position lights, anticollision lights, a landing light if operated for hire, an adequate electrical source and spare fuses [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]].

Legal is not the whole answer. An inoperative landing light makes night flying more hazardous even when the rule does not require one, so weigh any inoperative item against the expected conditions [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

callout.text: How to teach it: when a discrepancy turns up during preflight, let the learner decide first what to do, then discuss how good that choice was and what other options exist [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Ask what resources could help them judge it: their own knowledge, the POH, an instructor or an AMT [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

check.q: Before a day VFR lesson in a trainer certificated in 2005, your learner finds the anticollision (strobe) light inoperative and wants to placard it and go. What do you teach?
check.a: It cannot be deferred: for small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, the anticollision system is required for day VFR [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)]], and 91.213(d) excludes items 91.205 requires [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]. The only allowance in 91.205(b)(11) is to continue, after a failure, to a place where repairs can be made [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)]], and a training lesson is not that. Get it repaired before the lesson.

chunks.title: The walkaround: which items, why, and how to find defects

body.p: K3 has four sub-items. The first three live together on the walkaround, so teach them as one table you can carry to the airplane.

**Which items should be inspected (K3a).** The AFM/POH, or a checklist based on it, lists the items and the sequence, which often runs counterclockwise from the cabin entry [[24:42|AFH 2-5]] [[24:43|AFH 2-6]]. The inspection starts while walking up to the airplane [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

**The reasons for checking each item (K3b).** The visual preflight exists to reduce flight hazards [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Teach the reason with every item: learners who understand the purpose behind each step remember the steps better and can rebuild them when they forget [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].
**How to detect possible defects (K3c).** Look, touch, use a flashlight, and know what "normal" looks like on this airplane. A learner who only knows the item's name cannot find its defect.

head: Area
Which items (K3a)
Reason for checking (K3b)
How to detect defects (K3c)
rows: Walking up
Gear alignment, wing, fuselage and tail shape, stains, drips, puddles
Structural damage and leaks show first from a distance
Look for misalignment, distortion, skin damage, fuel or oil stains [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]
Door and cabin
Door fit and latches, belts and harnesses, seats and seat rails, windows
A poorly fitting door can mean structural damage; a crazed window can cut visibility to near zero in sunlight
Open, close and latch; check seat lock pins and rail holes worn oval; look for frayed belts, cracks and crazing [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]
Flight deck
Switches off, control lock removed, fuel selector in every position, gauges, gyros, compass
Confirms systems and instruments are usable before the engine runs

A stiff selector or one without legible positions or detents is unacceptable; hazing on a gyro face may mean a leak; a cloudy compass, bubbles or a partly filled case make the compass unusable [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]
Wings and tail
Spar lines, attach points, struts, leading edges, rivets, fiberglass tips and fairings
Load stresses concentrate on spar lines and attach points; cracks past a stop-drill can lead to in-flight failure

Ripples, bubbles, dents, creases or waves; cracked paint or black oxide film at rivets [[24:43|AFH 2-6]]; on composites, bubbles, hairline cracks, or a changed sound when tapped with a fingertip [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]
Fuel
Quantity in each tank, grade, water and sediment, vents, caps
Without the right quantity, grade and quality the engine will likely quit [[24:46|AFH 2-9]]; a blocked vent leads to fuel starvation [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]

Look in each tank because ramp slope and strut extension change capacity [[24:46|AFH 2-9]]; sample the strainer and each sump for color, water, dirt and odor; flashlight on the vent; a rush of air at the cap can mean a vent problem [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]
Oil
Level and color
Oil lubricates, carries heat and holds contaminants [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]
Read the dipstick; a cold engine reads higher than a warm one; oil that darkens fast after a change may mean cylinder problems [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]
Gear, tires, brakes
Struts, tires, wheels, brakes and lines, nose gear and shimmy damper, attach points
The airplane must be positively controllable on the ground [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]
Any leaking fluid is unacceptable; cuts, bulges, embedded objects or visible cords make a tire unairworthy; move the airplane to see the whole tire [[24:48|AFH 2-11]]
Engine and propeller
Cowling fasteners, spinner, blades, inside the cowling, exhaust, air filter
Losing the propulsion system leaves very little time to respond [[24:48|AFH 2-11]]
Nicks, cracks and erosion on blades; oil streaking from a hub toward the tip; nests or rags; white stains at exhaust leaks; darkened paint from excess heat [[24:49|AFH 2-12]]

body.p: The figure shows fiberglass cracks that were stop-drilled. A crack that has grown past its drilled hole, or a new crack next to it, may lead to in-flight failure [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]. Anything out of place goes to a properly rated mechanic [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

callout.text: Fuel and oil should not be left to line service without the pilot watching. Line personnel are professionals, but the pilot is responsible for the outcome, so monitor the grade and quantity added and check that every cap is secure [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

check.q: Your learner skips the fuel samples because "I watched the truck fill it." What do you teach?
check.a: Water can also come from condensation in the tanks, worn cap seals in rain, or the supplier's own tanks and trucks [[24:46|AFH 2-9]]. Drain the strainer and every sump to check grade, water, dirt and odor, and sump after refueling too [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

chunks.title: The associated regulations: the rules behind the walkaround

body.p: **The associated regulations (K3d).** A CFI applicant should be able to point at a part of the preflight and name the rule behind it. This table ties each rule to where it shows up:

head: Rule
What it requires
Where it shows up in the preflight
rows: Before every flight, become familiar with all available information, including runway lengths and takeoff and landing distances; away from the airport, also weather, fuel and alternatives [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]
Planning before the walkaround
Airworthy airplane; PIC decides it is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]]
The whole visual inspection
Comply with the AFM operating limitations, markings and placards; manual or approved material aboard; airplane identified under Part 45 [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]
Placards, instrument markings, POH in the airplane, data plate
Airworthiness and registration certificates aboard; airworthiness certificate displayed [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]]
Document check
Required equipment; inoperative equipment process [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205]] [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213]]
Flight deck check and any squawk
ELT attached and operable, inspected, battery current [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207]]
Records and the ELT itself
Owner keeps it airworthy; return to service after maintenance; annual, 100-hour and transponder checks [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413]]
Records review
Day VFR fuel to the first landing point plus 30 minutes; night plus 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151]]
Fuel quantity check
Alcohol, drugs and medical deficiency [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]] [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]]
Self-assessment

callout.text: How to teach it: tie the rule to the thing. Ground instruction works best when you point out the link between theory and practice, and a preflight can be taught on an actual airplane after it is first taught in the classroom [[25:172|AIH 9-2]]. Stand at the fuel cap and ask "which rule says how much fuel you need?" instead of quizzing section numbers at a desk.

check.q: Your learner thinks runway length only matters on cross-countries. Which rule says otherwise?
check.a: 14 CFR 91.103(b): for any flight, the PIC must know the runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance information [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

chunks.title: How to teach the walkaround with the checklist

body.p: The walkaround is a procedure, and the demonstration-performance method is built for teaching procedures and kinesthetic skills [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. In the airplane world it becomes the telling-and-doing technique:

head: Step
At the airplane
rows: Preparation (explanation)
On the ground before you walk out: the objective, how you will judge it, and safety items such as the propeller and fuel. Invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]
Instructor tells, instructor does
You do the walkaround with the checklist and say each step as you do it, in the same order you explained it. The learner watches [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner reads each item and tells you what to check and why; you do it. You hear their understanding before any habit forms [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner tells, learner does
The learner inspects and talks through each step. You watch for errors so faulty habits do not form [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Review against the objectives, give concrete suggestions, and try not to end on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

bullets: Demonstrate exactly the way you want it practiced, including every safety step. If your demonstration differs from your explanation, say so right away [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

Adjust to the learner. A preflight lesson for an experienced aircraft mechanic should be presented very differently from one for a learner with no aviation background, even though the content is the same [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].
Teach attention switching on purpose. Using a checklist means looking from the card to the part and back; a task put off for later is easily forgotten [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
Keep quiet while they practice. Avoid conversation and other distractions while a learner practices a skill [[25:80|AIH 3-29]].
Supervise. Overseeing the preflight is part of the instructor's job, so the hands-on task is done correctly [[25:106|AIH 5-3]].

callout.text: Learners treat their instructor as a role model and imitate the habits they see [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. Before each flight, talk about safety and why a proper preflight and the checklist matter [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. If you rush your own walkaround, you have just taught that too.

body.p: For S2, end every demonstration by saying the decision out loud: what the records showed, what the walkaround showed, and why the airplane is (or is not) in condition for safe flight and conforms to its type design. A learner reluctant to use the checklist can be reminded that pilots at every level use them, and the more advanced the airplane, the more they matter [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

check.q: Why add the "learner tells, instructor does" step instead of handing over the checklist right after your demonstration?
check.a: The learner can organize their thoughts without also doing the task, and you can check their understanding and fix any misunderstanding before they start forming habits. Because of primacy, the first time should be right [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Building the learner's own walkaround habit

body.p: The goal is a learner who does the full assessment, alone, every time. That takes habit, understanding, and a planned hand-off of responsibility.

bullets: Habits first. Insist on correct procedures from the outset; correct habits are much easier to build than faulty ones are to fix [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

Schemas. Learners build a mental pattern, a schema, for the preflight, which helps them know what to expect [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. The same schema can make them miss something that does not fit it, so vary the airplanes and the conditions.
Watch for overlearning. A checklist can become so automatic that reciting the items no longer triggers the thinking and looking they are meant to trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

Use reminders and routines. Errors drop when checklists are used actively and standard procedures are followed, and when the pilot raises their awareness under time pressure, changes in routine, fatigue or lack of recent practice [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].
Slow is fine. Hurrying causes slips; working at a comfortable pace reduces errors [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].

body.p: Hand over the decisions in stages and grade them. The AIH grades SRM with Explain (the learner can describe the risks but needs prompting), Practice (the learner applies them, with quick coaching), and Manage/Decide (the learner gathers the data, weighs options and decides with no instructor intervention), plus Not Observed for events not done [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Grading should be progressive across lessons [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

Solo readiness is usually judged when you watch the learner from preflight to engine start to shutdown and they perform consistently without help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. Make the postflight part of the habit too: a postflight inspection can find hazards before the next person flies the airplane [[30:22|RMH 3-4]], and the AFH lists what to look for, from oil streaks and fuel stains to tires and brakes [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

callout.text: S3 and S4 belong in the habit, not only on the checkride. Ask the learner to say their self-assessment and their environment check aloud before every lesson, then ask "what has changed since you planned this?" Making the 3P discussion part of every preflight builds risk management by repetition [[25:16|AIH 1-12]].

check.q: Your post-solo learner recites the whole checklist from memory at top speed. Why might that worry you, and how can you test it?
check.a: The checklist may have become automatic, with the words no longer triggering real inspection [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. Stop at random items and ask what a defect there would look like and why it matters; understanding the purpose of each step is what lets learners rebuild it [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

chunks.title: Environmental factors: weather, terrain, route selection and obstructions

body.p: K4 asks for four environmental factors. Teach each one with the questions the learner should ask:

head: Factor
What to assess
rows: Weather

Current ceiling and visibility, with higher minimums in mountains; the chance it differs from the forecast, with an alternate plan; crosswind; strong winds aloft over mountains; thunderstorms; icing, the temperature-dewpoint spread and whether a safe descent is possible all along the route [[25:9|AIH 1-5]]
Terrain
Safe altitudes picked in advance from chart altitudes and MEFs, especially at night or in low visibility [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]; high density altitude hurts takeoff, climb and landing [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]
Route selection

An engine failure makes nearby airports supremely important; shorter or obstructed fields; survival gear over remote areas; TFRs along the route [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]. Plan to go around, above or below a hazard, or change the departure time [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]
Obstructions

At and below 200 ft AGL many towers and wires are unmarked, unlit or uncharted; guy wires reach about 1,500 ft out, so avoid skeletal structures horizontally by at least 2,000 ft; many wind turbines now exceed 499 ft AGL [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]]

body.p: Weather also sits on the airplane. Remove all frost, snow and ice during the preflight, because even very small amounts can hurt the wing's aerodynamics. A heated hangar works, but the airplane must be dry before it goes back out so the water does not refreeze [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4]].

**S4: continue to assess.** The assessment does not end at the tiedown. Situational awareness runs until the airplane is secured again [[24:38|AFH 2-1]], and the 3P model is a continuous loop: perceive, process, perform, then start again because your own action changed the situation [[25:16|AIH 1-12]].

callout.text: How to teach it: prompt the learner to spot hazards and say their thinking aloud, for example naming collision hazards and a safe landing spot before a ground reference maneuver [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. And do not create hazards by teaching at the wrong time or place, such as stalls below a cloud layer with too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

check.q: Your learner wants to follow a river to the practice area at low altitude to stay under the haze. What obstruction risk do you raise?
check.a: Wires often span natural flyways such as rivers, and at and below 200 ft AGL many lines and towers are not marked, lighted or charted, and new ones may not be on the chart yet [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]].

chunks.title: Teaching risk management: pilot, aircraft, environment

body.p: Risk management should start at the very beginning of training, be built into every flight lesson rather than taught separately, and appear in every preflight and postflight briefing. As experience grows, the learner should lead those discussions [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

Identify, assess, mitigate. Coach the learner to use the PAVE buckets methodically and to check every sub-element in each [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Assessment is the hardest step, so lead it at first with clear examples, such as an engine failure after takeoff [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Then use the matrix:

Mitigate high (red) and serious (yellow) risks. Medium (green) risks may be mitigated where possible, on the principle of not accepting unnecessary risk [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. TEAM names the choices: transfer, eliminate, accept, mitigate [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

head: Risk
Hazards special to instruction
How the instructor mitigates
rows: R1 Pilot
The learner is less proficient; the instructor may be unfamiliar with the airplane or avionics; both have aeromedical risks [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]
Learn the airplane and avionics before instructing; IMSAFE on yourself; encourage learners to disclose problems early [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
R2 Aircraft
Unknown inoperative items or overdue inspections; limited payload; marginal performance at high density altitude [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]
Check status and discrepancies before the flight and resolve them with maintenance [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]; thorough preflight and postflight inspections and good maintenance [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]
R3 Environment
Crowded practice airspace, haze, complex airspace, and hazards created by maneuvers such as full stalls or simulated engine failures [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Involve the learner; in marginal VFR, change the lesson to the pattern, a simulator or ground school, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]

body.p: Build it in blocks [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]:

bullets: Pre-solo: introduce a non-numerical FRAT and demonstrate it during the first few flights. By first solo, the learner can do a basic risk analysis.
Post-solo: the learner does the analysis with occasional coaching; you review it for every solo, and the learner debriefs you on risk afterward.
Cross-country: a full risk analysis for every dual and solo cross-country, which you review and approve like any other planning.

callout.text: Use numerical FRATs with caution. A low score can hide one extreme risk, such as embedded thunderstorms across the route, that the form's list never asks about [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

check.q: Your learner rates a risk medium (green) and says, "Green means do nothing." How do you refine that?
check.a: Medium and low risks do not normally require mitigation [[25:8|AIH 1-4]], but instructors should teach that medium risks may still be mitigated where possible, following the principle of not accepting unnecessary risk [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

chunks.title: External pressures: the learner's and the instructor's

body.p: External pressures are influences from outside the flight that push to complete it, often at the cost of safety: someone waiting, a passenger the pilot does not want to disappoint, wanting to show off qualifications or impress someone, get-home-itis, a goal-completion habit, and pride about one's skill level [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]. Managing them is the single most important key to risk management, because this is the one category that can make a pilot ignore all the others [[25:11|AIH 1-7]].
Personal standard operating procedures give the pressure a release valve [[25:11|AIH 1-7]]:

bullets: Allow time for an extra fuel stop or a weather landing.
Have a backup plan, such as an airline reservation, for must-be-there trips.
Tell the people waiting that you may be late, and how you will let them know.
Carry a small overnight kit so there is no pressure to get home.

body.p: Learners bring their own: scheduling problems, made worse by aircraft and weather delays, plus work, family and money pressures that cause distraction and anxiety [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. External pressures can create the most insidious hazards. The instructor eases schedule worries, can switch from the airplane to the classroom, and can end a lesson early if the learner seems anxious about time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Application: the instructor has external pressures too, such as a full schedule or a checkride date. The AIH's list includes the general urge to complete the goal [[25:10|AIH 1-6]], and that applies to whoever sits in the right seat.

callout.text: Personal minimums are set at home, not on the ramp: never make a minimum less restrictive while planning a specific flight, or the external pressures will be the ones deciding [[25:206|AIH D-1]].

Role play works here. Play a passenger or a boss who pushes to go and have the learner say no, with an alternative, out loud. Role playing a learner's reactions is also how instructor applicants practice [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

check.q: Your learner's practical test is tomorrow, and today's last practice flight looks marginal. The learner insists they need it. How do you handle the pressure?
check.a: Name it as an external pressure, then use the AIH options: change the schedule, switch to classroom or simulator training, or end the lesson early if time pressure is showing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Being ready for and accepting delays is the key [[25:11|AIH 1-7]].

body.p: Aviation security is one of the common special emphasis items the AIH lists for flight instructors to cover [[25:164|AIH 8-6]], and the Aviator's Model Code of Conduct, which the AIH recommends to instructors, has a section on security [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. On the preflight it shows up in four places:

bullets: On the ramp: passengers move only as directed, and anyone not under your direct supervision gets an escort for safety and ramp security. Supervise baggage loading [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

Restricted areas: a SIDA needs an airport-issued badge, and entering one without authorization and displayed ID is prohibited. Violators may be reported to the TSA or airport security and fined, so brief passengers [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]] [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Reporting and ID: report suspicious activity through AOPA's Airport Watch Program, 866-427-3287, and show your airman or medical certificate to the TSA on request [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Planning: check NOTAMs for TFRs and National Security Areas. Pilots who ignore national security procedures may be intercepted, detained and interviewed [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]].

body.p: After the flight, install control locks and anti-theft security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Pitot tube covers, cowling inlet covers, gust locks and propeller security locks add safety and security to the airplane [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

callout.text: Involve the learner: teach them to help with the training environment items, such as airspace, NOTAMs and TFRs, as part of the dual lesson [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Security then becomes a planning habit, not a sign on a fence.

check.q: Your learner props open a ramp gate marked as a SIDA to carry the headsets out. What do you teach?
check.a: Movement into a SIDA without authorization and displayed ID is prohibited, and violators may be reported to the TSA [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]] [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]]. An open gate lets anyone in; close it, and treat ramp access as part of the preflight.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Checklist recited, not used
Fast, rhythmic readout; eyes on the card, not the airplane [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Ask at random items what a defect would look like and why it matters [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]
Lost place after an interruption
The fuel truck arrives, the checklist goes down, and the learner resumes one item later [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Teach a standard way to handle interruptions; standard procedures reduce error [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. Application: go back to the last item you are sure was done
Gauges trusted over tanks
The learner reads the gauges and moves on
Look in each tank; ramp slope and strut extension change the level [[24:46|AFH 2-9]]
One fuel sample, or none
Only the strainer drained, or water beads dumped and forgotten
Drain every sump; if water appears, keep sampling until none shows [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]
Hurried, cursory inspection
A short walkaround on a busy day
Time pressure causes slips [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]; a cursory inspection to save time can let a problem show up later [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]
Airplane checked, pilot not
No self-assessment before the walkaround
Make the personal checklist part of every preflight [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]
Waiting for the instructor to decide
The learner finds a squawk and looks at you
Let the learner choose first, then discuss options [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Assessment stops at engine start
No new look when weather, timing or the plan changes
Situational awareness lasts until the airplane is secured [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]; rerun the 3P loop [[25:16|AIH 1-12]]

body.p: Instructor errors are just as common:

bullets: Teaching the first preflight as a list of disasters, which can scare a new learner off [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].
Demonstrating differently from the explanation without saying so [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
Rushing your own walkaround in front of learners, who imitate what they see [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].
Criticizing without explaining. Errors that are not identified and explained tend to be repeated through faulty practice [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

check.q: Your learner does a careful walkaround, then admits in the run-up that they had a migraine this morning and took medicine for it. Which error from the table is this, and what is the fix?
check.a: Airplane checked, pilot not. Make the personal checklist part of every preflight, before the walkaround [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]; IMSAFE asks about any medicine that might affect judgment or cause drowsiness [[25:12|AIH 1-8]].

scenario.title: The first dual cross-country after solo
scenario.setup: It is a Saturday in late October. You will fly a dual cross-country with a post-solo learner in the flight school's two-seat trainer: 70 NM to a towered airport that sits near a large football stadium, departing at 0900. The learner worked a late shift and slept about 5 hours. The trainer spent the night outside under clear skies and has light frost on the wings. The discrepancy sheet shows the left fuel gauge written up two days ago, with no maintenance sign-off. The learner's father is driving to the destination to meet you both for lunch. The forecast calls for ceilings lowering to 2,500 ft by midafternoon.

questions.q: Pilot: how do you handle the learner's 5 hours of sleep, and what about you?
questions.a: Run IMSAFE on both of you; the P applies to learner and instructor [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Fatigue may not show until serious errors happen [[25:12|AIH 1-8]], so ask open questions and watch for acute fatigue signs such as inattention and timing errors [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. If they appear, change to a ground lesson or reschedule [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: Aircraft: can the left fuel gauge be deferred so you can go?
questions.a: No. A fuel gauge for each tank is required for day VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]], and 91.213(d) does not allow deferring items 91.205 requires [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]. Settle it with maintenance before the preflight [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and let the learner work out that answer first [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

questions.q: Aircraft: the gauge is fixed. What about the frost?
questions.a: Remove all of it before flight; even very small amounts can hurt the wing's aerodynamics. If you use a heated hangar, make sure the airplane is dry before it comes out so the water does not refreeze [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4]].

questions.q: Environment: what do the stadium and the lowering ceiling add to the plan?
questions.a: Check NOTAMs for TFRs near the stadium during planning [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]] [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]. For the ceiling, consider changing the departure time or planning the return earlier [[30:40|RMH 5-2]], and keep alternatives ready in case the weather differs from the forecast [[25:9|AIH 1-5]].

questions.q: External pressures: the father is already driving. How do you take the pressure off?
questions.a: Tell him now that you may be late or may not come, and how you will let him know; be ready to accept a delay [[25:11|AIH 1-7]]. Managing the expectations of the people waiting is the RMH approach [[30:40|RMH 5-2]].

questions.q: Teaching: how do you make this the learner's assessment rather than yours?
questions.a: Cross-country training calls for a full risk analysis by the learner on every flight, reviewed and approved by you [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. Let the learner lead the discussion as experience grows [[25:186|AIH 10-2]], decide first on each discrepancy, then discuss [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "inspect the airplane with reference to an appropriate checklist." There is no numeric tolerance. The examiner watches you follow the AFM/POH checklist sequence [[24:42|AFH 2-5]] while saying, for each item, what you check, why, and what a defect would look like, the way you would demonstrate to a learner [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
skills.practice: Do a full walkaround with another applicant playing a new learner. Explain every item without skipping, then switch roles and have them tell while you do.

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "verify the airplane is in condition for safe flight and conforms to its type design." The examiner wants the records and documents checked [[24:40|AFH 2-3]] [[24:41|AFH 2-4]], conformity tied to the equipment list and approved alterations [[24:25|AFH 1-4]], any inoperative item worked through 91.213 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]], and a clear go or no-go stated out loud.
skills.practice: Pull the records for your training airplane and build a one-page status summary like AFH Figure 2-4. Then have a friend invent squawks and talk through each one.

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "perform self-assessment." Say your IMSAFE and capability check out loud [[25:12|AIH 1-8]] [[30:22|RMH 3-4]], compare against written personal minimums [[25:206|AIH D-1]], and explain how you would coach a learner through theirs.
skills.practice: Fill in the AIH Personal Minimums Checklist for yourself, then practice a two-minute self-assessment briefing you could give at the start of any lesson.

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "continue to assess the environment for safe flight." Show that the assessment does not stop at the walkaround: update the weather, terrain, route and obstruction picture as things change and explain the 3P loop as you go [[25:16|AIH 1-12]] [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].
skills.practice: On every flight this month, say aloud at engine start, takeoff, cruise and before landing what has changed in the environment and what it means for the plan.

quiz.q: Beyond the 91.205 list, where does a pilot find the equipment required for this particular airplane to be airworthy?
options: The last annual inspection entry
The equipment list in the AFM/POH
The registration certificate
The airworthiness certificate displayed in the cabin
quiz.why: The AFM/POH equipment list, made during certification, identifies the items required for airworthiness [[24:25|AFH 1-4]].

quiz.q: You start instructing at a new flight school in its airplanes. Besides each airplane's official airworthiness status, what does the AIH say you should know and review before you instruct?
options: The school's procedure for reporting and fixing discrepancies, and its current discrepancy report
Only the due dates of each airplane's next annual and 100-hour inspections, from the school's records
The fuel supplier's contamination test records and the date its fuel truck was last sampled
Nothing more; the school's mechanic is responsible for everything beyond the airworthiness status
quiz.why: Unless instructing in their own aircraft, instructors should know the operator's procedures for reporting and correcting discrepancies and review the current discrepancy report [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.207(f)(3), the ELT requirement does not apply to training operations conducted entirely within what distance of the airport where the local flights began?
options: 25 NM
50 NM
75 NM
10 NM
quiz.why: The exception covers training operations entirely within a 50 NM radius of that airport [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]].

quiz.q: Small dark specks in a fuel sample most likely come from what?
options: Jet fuel mixed into the AVGAS
Clear water beads from condensation
Deteriorating rubber seals or tank sealant
Normal blue dye settling out of the 100LL
quiz.why: Deteriorating rubber from seals and sealant may show up in the sample as small dark specks [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks why the school fills the tanks after the last flight of the day. What does the AFH give as the reason?
options: Less room for water to condense, and slower aging of rubber tanks and sealant
Full tanks are heavier, so the airplane is less likely to move in a gusty overnight wind
Fuel is cheaper in the evening
It saves the next pilot from waiting for the fuel truck before the first flight
quiz.why: The more fuel in the tanks, the less room for condensation, and full tanks slow the aging of rubber tanks and sealant [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

quiz.q: During the walkaround, where should your learner look most closely for ripples, dents or creases, because load stresses concentrate there?
options: The center of the large fuselage and wing skin panels between the rivet rows
Spar lines and wing, stabilizer and gear attach points
The wheel fairings and the nose bowl around the spinner
The cabin windows
quiz.why: Load-related stresses concentrate along spar lines and attach points, so deformities there may mean internal damage [[24:43|AFH 2-6]].

quiz.q: What is the main danger of attention switching during a checklist preflight?
options: The learner spends too long looking at the airplane instead of the card
It doubles the time of the preflight
Checklists cannot be used outdoors
A task put off for later is easily forgotten
quiz.why: When one task is postponed while switching between tasks, it is very easy to forget it completely [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

quiz.q: A fiberglass wingtip crack was stop-drilled at the last inspection. Today it has grown past the drilled hole. What does the AFH say?
options: Acceptable on a fiberglass tip, since it is a non-structural part of the wing
Stop-drilling is a permanent repair, so growth past the hole is cosmetic and can wait
It may lead to in-flight failure; have a rated mechanic look at it before flight
Drill a new stop hole at the end of the crack yourself, then fly as planned
quiz.why: Cracks that continue past a stop-drilled location, or new cracks next to it, may lead to in-flight failure [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]; refer it to a properly rated mechanic [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

quiz.q: On the cabin check, what does the AFH say to confirm about the seats?
options: Only that the cushions are dry and the carpet under them is affixed
They slide freely along the whole rail, which shows the rails are lubricated
They latch into the rails with the lock pins, and the rail holes are not worn oval
Nothing; the seats and rails are checked only at the annual inspection
quiz.why: Seats should latch properly into the seat rails through the seat lock pins, and the seat rail holes should not be abnormally worn to an oval shape [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

quiz.q: Many wind turbines now exceed what height, according to the AIM?
options: 2,000 ft AGL
499 ft AGL
1,000 ft AGL
200 ft AGL
quiz.why: Many wind turbines exceed 499 ft AGL, which may affect minimum safe VFR altitudes [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4]].

final_quiz.q: On the walkaround your learner finds a small cut in the nose tire with cords showing. The tire holds air and today's lesson is dual. What does the AFH say?
options: Visible cords make the tire unairworthy; it must be fixed before flight
Fine for a dual lesson, as long as the pressure is right and the cut is small
Fine until the next annual inspection, since tire wear is a maintenance item
Fly, but keep the nosewheel light on takeoff and landing to protect it
final_quiz.why: Cuts, bulges, imbedded foreign objects and visible cords render a tire unairworthy, and moving the airplane slightly lets the pilot see the whole tire [[24:48|AFH 2-11]].

final_quiz.q: Before a day VFR lesson in a trainer with no MEL, the learner finds the cabin dome light inoperative. It is not on the equipment list or KOEL, not required by 91.205 and not tied to an AD. What must happen before takeoff?
options: Obtain a letter of authorization so the school can fly under an MEL for this one item
Nothing: an item not required by 91.205, the equipment list or an AD needs no placard or entry
Get a special flight permit from the FSDO to fly the airplane to a repair station
Deactivate and placard it Inoperative (or remove it), and a qualified person finds it is no hazard
final_quiz.why: 91.213(d) still requires removal or deactivation with a placard, and a determination by an appropriately rated pilot or maintenance person that it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

final_quiz.q: A usually careful learner skips the oil cap and the fuel vent, misreads two items, and snaps at you when corrected. Which fits the AIH best?
options: A learning plateau; keep the lesson going so the learner pushes through it
Signs of acute fatigue; stop and assess the learner before going on
Overlearning of the checklist; have the learner read it faster
Normal first-lesson nerves that will pass once the engine is running
final_quiz.why: Acute fatigue shows as inattention, neglect of secondary tasks, loss of accuracy and irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]], and fatigue may not be apparent until serious errors are made [[25:12|AIH 1-8]].

final_quiz.q: When your learner cracks open the left fuel cap, there is a strong rush of air. What does the AFH say this can mean?
options: The tank was overfilled, so the cap was holding back fuel pressure
Normal: vapor pressure builds up in every sealed fuel tank overnight
There could be a serious problem with the fuel vent system
Normal on a cold morning, since cold air in the tank always shrinks
final_quiz.why: If there is a rush of air when the fuel tank cap is cracked, there could be a serious problem with the vent system; a blocked vent can lead to fuel starvation and engine failure [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner soloed last week. Per the AIH, what should risk management look like now?
options: The learner does it alone for every solo, and you stop reviewing it unless asked
You keep doing every risk analysis yourself until the learner's practical test is done
The learner does it with occasional coaching, you review it for every solo, and the learner debriefs you
The learner fills out a numerical FRAT only for solo cross-countries, and you sign it
final_quiz.why: After first solo, the learner performs the risk analysis with occasional coaching, the instructor reviews it for all solo flights, and the learner debriefs the instructor [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner orders fuel and oil, then waits in the FBO while the line crew services the airplane. What does the AFH suggest?
options: Nothing more: line personnel are trained aviation professionals, so the fuel slip is proof enough
Sump the tanks after the truck leaves; that check takes the place of watching the servicing
Check only the fuel grade on the receipt, since the oil quantity is a maintenance item
Watch the servicing: confirm the right grade and quantity went in and every cap is secure
final_quiz.why: Fuel and oil should not be left to line personnel without the pilot's oversight; the pilot monitors that the correct quantity, quality and grade go in and that all caps are securely replaced [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: The airplane was fueled to the top on a sloped ramp with the nose strut low. Both gauges read full. What should your learner do?
options: Look in each tank, since attitude on the ramp changes capacity
Trust the gauges, since both read full and the airplane was just fueled
Add 10 percent to the planned burn to cover any gauge error
Sump only the strainer, since a fresh load has no water
final_quiz.why: Strut extension and ramp slope change the airplane's attitude and fuel capacity, so always confirm the gauges by looking in each tank [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

final_quiz.q: After setting the checklist down to talk to the fuel truck driver, your learner picks it up and resumes at the oil check, skipping the left wing. What kind of error is this?
options: Overlearning, from reciting the checklist too fast
A mistake, an error of thought from a faulty plan
Negative transfer from a different airplane's checklist
A slip, an error of action from an interruption
final_quiz.why: Slips are errors of action, often neglecting to do something [[25:84|AIH 3-33]], and a classic one is resuming a checklist at a later point after an interruption [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

final_quiz.q: Your new learner is an experienced aircraft mechanic. How should you teach the preflight?
options: Skip the walkaround items they already inspect every day as a mechanic
Have them teach it to you, since their knowledge exceeds the POH
Exactly the same presentation and wording as for any new learner
Same required content, presented differently for their background
final_quiz.why: The instruction needed is the same, but a presentation meaningful to an AMT differs from one for a learner with no aviation experience [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

final_quiz.q: On a cold morning before the first flight, the dipstick reads a little higher than it did after yesterday's last flight. No oil was added. What does the AFH say?
options: Unusual: the level should read the same hot or cold, so have maintenance look at it
Expected: a cold engine reads higher on the dipstick than a warm one just shut down
Skip the dipstick on cold mornings and check the oil level after the run-up instead
Drain some oil before start, since a cold engine must not be run above the low mark
final_quiz.why: If the engine is cold, the dipstick shows a higher level than if the engine was warm and recently shut down; the oil level is checked during each preflight and rechecked with each refueling [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner skips NOTAMs for a local flight because "we're not going anywhere." Which is correct?
options: NOTAMs matter only on cross-countries, because a local flight stays in airspace the learner already knows
Only IFR flights must check NOTAMs, since a VFR pilot can see and avoid any restricted area
Check them for TFRs and security areas: 91.103 covers every flight, and violators may be intercepted
ATC or the CTAF will warn any pilot about a new TFR before the airplane reaches it
final_quiz.why: Under 91.103 pilots must become familiar with all available information, should check NOTAMs for TFRs and National Security Areas, and may be intercepted or detained for noncompliance [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]] [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

final_quiz.q: At 0700 the trainer has a thin layer of frost on the upper wing. Your learner says it will blow off during the takeoff roll. What do you teach?
options: Remove all of it before flight; even small amounts can hurt the wing's aerodynamics
Fine if the learner plans for a longer takeoff run and a faster rotation speed
Only frost on the lower wing surface matters, since the upper surface dries in the sun
Fine below 2,000 ft density altitude, where the extra drag is small
final_quiz.why: During the preflight, remove all frost, snow and ice, because even very small amounts may adversely affect the wing [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4]].

final_quiz.q: The school's trainer had its ELT removed for repair 75 days ago. The records show the removal entry (date, make, model, serial number and reason) and an "ELT not installed" placard is in view. You plan a 120 NM dual cross-country. May you fly?
options: No; beyond 50 NM a removed ELT must be reinstalled before flight, whatever the records show
Only if the flight stays within 25 NM of the airport, under the training exception
Only with a special flight permit, since the removal is past the 60-day limit
Yes; the temporary-removal exception allows up to 90 days with the entry and placard
final_quiz.why: An aircraft may operate while its ELT is temporarily removed, with a records entry and an "ELT not installed" placard, for no more than 90 days after removal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]].

takeaways: Airworthy has two parts: conforms to type design and in condition for safe operation; the PIC decides the second part on every flight.
Assess the pilot before the airplane, and in dual the P means both of you.
Teach each walkaround item with three answers: what to check, why, and what a defect looks like.
Tie every rule to the part of the airplane or the record where it shows up.
Use telling-and-doing at the airplane, and let the learner decide first when a squawk appears.
Build risk management in blocks, from a non-numerical FRAT before solo to a full analysis you approve on cross-countries.
The assessment never stops: keep updating weather, route and pressures until the airplane is secured.
cfi_notes: AI.III.B (Airworthiness Requirements) covers inspections, ADs and records in depth. In this Task the examiner is looking at how you apply them at the airplane and teach them during a preflight.

AFH 2-3 says the ELT inspection is due "within the last 12 months" and PHAK 9-9 says the transponder test is due "within the 24 months." 14 CFR 91.207(d) and 91.413 say 12 and 24 calendar months. Teach the CFR wording; it moves the due date to the end of the month.
The RMH notes that some publications use the E in IMSAFE for Eating instead of Emotion (RMH 3-5). The AIH and PHAK use Emotion. Teach Emotion and mention food and water for long days.

PHAK 2-8 says one ounce of liquor, one beer or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills; the AIH says only "a small amount." Neither changes 91.17. Teach the rule and the 24-hour question in IMSAFE.

The sources do not say whether a dual lesson in a school airplane is an operation "for hire" under 91.205(c)(4) (night landing light). Do not invent an answer: ask the school and the FSDO. Application: until you have their answer, the conservative choice is not to defer an inoperative landing light on a paid night lesson.

91.207(f)(3) surprises learners: local training within 50 NM does not need an ELT. Use it to show why the exact wording of a rule matters. Teach learners to check whether a flight really stays inside that exception.

The AIH says the final go or no-go choice in training belongs to the instructor (AIH 1-28), yet the learner should decide first. Make your decision visible and explain it, so the learner sees judgment, not just a veto.
Practice for the checkride by role play: another CFI plays a learner who skips items, misreads the fuel sample or pushes to go, and you correct them (AIH 4-7).
Your own walkaround is a demonstration every time a learner is watching. Do it the way you want it copied (AIH 8-6).
gaps: Checklist order, sump locations and order, approved fuel grades, oil limits, frost allowances and the equipment list or KOEL come only from the training airplane's AFM/POH.
The flight school's discrepancy reporting and grounding procedures are operator procedures, not in the FAA sources; the AIH only says to know and follow them.
14 CFR Part 3 (the 3.5(a) airworthy definition) is not in the resource set; it is cited through AFH 2-1.
The sources give no standard for how many supervised preflights a learner needs before solo; that is the instructor's judgment, guided by consistent performance (AIH 8-5).
TSA general aviation security guidance and 49 CFR 1540 are not in the resources; security content here comes from the AIM, AFH and AIH.
The ACS skill elements for this Task have no numeric tolerances.

activities.title: Read the airworthiness summary
activities.intro: Drag each requirement to the item on the checklist it describes.

pins.label: Must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance
Not needed for a local flight in a light trainer
Includes the airspeed indicator's color arcs
Required only if the airworthiness standards call for it
Inspection due by calendar for every airplane, for hire or not
Required at night only when operated for hire

activities.why: The airworthiness certificate must be displayed at the entrance [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]]. The radio station license is only for flights outside the U.S. or airplanes over 12,500 lb; operating limitations may be the AFM/POH, placards, instrument markings or a combination; the compass card is needed if required by the airworthiness standards; the data plate falls under Part 45 [[24:41|AFH 2-4]], and 91.9(c) requires the airplane to be identified under Part 45 [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]. The annual is due within the preceding 12 calendar months for any operation [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]. Landing light: night, for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].

activities.title: True or false: what the walkaround finds
activities.intro: Your learner makes these claims during a walkaround. True or false?

cards.s: On a controllable-pitch propeller, oil streaking from the hub toward the tip points to a hub leak.
cards.why: Hub oil leaks tend to stream from the hub toward the tip [[24:49|AFH 2-12]].

cards.s: White stains around the exhaust stacks are normal and need no follow-up.
cards.why: White stains can come from exhaust leaks at the cylinder head or cracks in the stacks [[24:49|AFH 2-12]].

cards.s: A slow drip from a brake line is acceptable if the pedal feels firm.
cards.why: Any amount of leaking fluid is unacceptable; brake lines should be dry [[24:48|AFH 2-11]].

cards.s: A severely crazed window is only a problem at night.
cards.why: A dirty, scratched or crazed window can give near zero visibility from light refraction at certain sun angles [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

cards.s: A fuel selector that is stiff but reaches every position is acceptable.
cards.why: Stiff selectors, or ones with illegible positions or no detents, are unacceptable [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].

cards.s: An isolated patch of darkened, oxidized paint on the engine may mean too much heat in that area.
cards.why: The AFH lists it as a possible sign of excessive heat [[24:49|AFH 2-12]].

activities.title: Work the fuel and ELT numbers
activities.intro: Use the rules and source values. Round as asked.

items.q: A day VFR dual lesson is planned for 1.4 hours at 8.0 gallons per hour, landing back home. What is the minimum fuel at takeoff to meet the VFR reserve rule? Ignore taxi fuel.
items.why: Day VFR needs fuel to the first point of landing plus 30 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. (1.4 + 0.5) x 8.0 = 1.9 x 8.0 = 15.2 gal.

items.q: A night lesson is planned for 1.0 hour at 7.0 gallons per hour, landing back home. Minimum fuel at takeoff? Ignore taxi fuel.

A two-seat trainer has a maximum weight of 1,670 lb and an empty weight of 1,180 lb. You weigh 185 lb, your learner 220 lb, and bags 15 lb. How many gallons of fuel can you carry? Use 6 lb per gallon and round down to 0.1.
items.why: Gasoline weighs 6 lb per gallon [[1:246|PHAK 10-2]]. 1,670 - 1,180 - 185 - 220 - 15 = 70 lb; 70 / 6 = 11.67, so 11.6 gal. Application: compare with the 15.2 gal above. Two-place trainers often cannot carry full fuel with two aboard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

items.q: An ELT battery has a manufacturer's useful life of 6 years. After how many months must it be replaced, if it is never used?
items.why: Batteries are replaced when 50 percent of their useful life has expired [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(2)]]. 6 years x 12 = 72 months; 72 x 0.5 = 36 months.

activities.title: Put the preflight assessment in order
activities.intro: Your learner is preparing for a dual lesson in a school airplane. Put the steps in the order the AIH and AFH describe.
steps: The day before the lesson, check the airplane's airworthiness status and discrepancy list with the school
At the airport, review the logbooks or the airworthiness status summary
Note the airplane's general appearance while walking up
Confirm the required documents are aboard
Inspect the cabin door and the cabin
Walk around the exterior in the POH sequence
activities.why: Status and discrepancies are settled before the scheduled flight and before the preflight [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Once the logbooks show the airplane meets its requirements, the visual inspection begins while approaching, then documents, then the cabin door and interior [[24:41|AFH 2-4]], the flight deck items [[24:42|AFH 2-5]] and the exterior sequence from the POH [[24:43|AFH 2-6]].

activities.title: What is this defect telling you?
activities.intro: Your learner points at each finding. Match it to what it may indicate.

pairs.l: Door hard to close, latches stiff
pairs.r: Misalignment of the doorpost, possibly structural damage

pairs.l: Hazing on a mechanical gyro instrument face
Black oxide film around a rivet head
pairs.r: The rivet working loose in its hole

pairs.l: Ripples or creases along a spar line
Old-looking fuel stains under the wing
Bubbles or fine hairline cracks on a composite wing
pairs.r: Possible delamination of spar to skin

activities.why: Door fit [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]; gyro hazing [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]; rivets and spar lines [[24:43|AFH 2-6]]; fuel stains, no matter how old [[24:46|AFH 2-9]]; composite delamination [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

activities.title: Which PAVE bucket?
activities.intro: These hazards come up before a dual lesson. Sort each into its PAVE bucket.

items.t: You have never flown this trainer's new avionics
The trainer cannot carry full fuel with both of you aboard
A discrepancy entry has no maintenance sign-off
Haze in a crowded practice area
Practicing full stalls can lead to an inadvertent spin
The learner's practical test is booked for tomorrow
The learner's boss needs them back at work by noon

activities.why: Pilot risks include aeromedical issues and instructor unfamiliarity with avionics; aircraft risks include limited payload and unknown discrepancies [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Environmental risks include crowded, hazy airspace and maneuvers such as full stalls; external pressures include scheduling and work demands [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

activities.title: A morning dual lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You have an 0800 dual lesson in the school trainer with a pre-solo learner: slow flight and stalls in the practice area. Choose what you would do at each point.

steps.s: 0745: your learner arrives after a double shift with about 4 hours of sleep and says, "I'm fine, let's go."
options: Fly as planned; the learner says they are fine
Fly, but you do all the maneuvers
Let the learner decide alone and say nothing
Talk through IMSAFE together and change to a ground lesson or reschedule
steps.why: Fatigue may not show until serious errors happen [[25:12|AIH 1-8]], and the instructor must be tuned in to the learner's aeromedical state [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Switching to classroom training or rescheduling are AIH options [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: Two days later, rested. The discrepancy list shows yesterday's entry: "stall warning inoperative," with no maintenance entry.
options: Fly; you will watch the airspeed closely
Ask the learner what they would do, then resolve it with maintenance before the preflight
Write INOP on a sticky note and go
Do the stalls without the warning to make them realistic
steps.why: Let the learner decide first, then discuss [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Airworthiness questions are resolved with maintenance before the preflight [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and a deferral is legal only if the item is not required and the 91.213(d) steps are done [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

steps.s: Repaired and signed off. On the walkaround, the first sample from the left sump has clear beads at the bottom of the cup.
options: Pour it out; one sample is enough
Sample again until no water or contamination appears; call maintenance if it keeps coming
Go, since water is normal after rain
Switch to the right tank for the whole flight
steps.why: If water is found, keep sampling until none appears; significant or consistent water calls for maintenance [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

steps.s: Ready to go, the ceiling at the practice area is reported 2,800 ft broken and lowering.
options: Do the stalls just under the clouds
Go anyway; the forecast may be wrong
Coach the learner through the risks, then switch to pattern work or ground training
Climb above the layer for the stalls
steps.why: In marginal weather, coach the learner to identify risks and change the plan to the pattern, a simulator or ground school, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Teaching stalls below a cloud layer creates a hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: After the pattern lesson, the learner shuts down and heads for the car.
options: Do a postflight walkaround, install control and security locks, then debrief risk management together
Let them go; the school will handle it
Only refuel the airplane
Debrief by text message later
steps.why: Postflight inspections find hazards before the next flight [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]; secure the airplane with control and anti-theft locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; and risk management belongs in every postflight briefing [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].
